The Corporate Reputation
Strategy System
THE COMPLETE DOCUMENT LIBRARY
Thirteen documents, one volume: the master runbook, the navigation map and language  
standard, the nine step guides, and the two system documents.
July 2026
Contents of this volume
In reading order. Each document begins on its own cover page.
# Document Role
1 CD-S-002 — Corporate Reputation Strategy (Integrated Master) The runbook the team follows — 11 steps, gates, 
deliverables
2 Guide Index & Navigation Map The front door — how it all fits, plus the language 
standard
3 Client Intake & Briefing Toolkit Step guide · Steps 1–3 (brief, debrief, final brief)
4 Research & Audit Guide Step guide · Step 4
5 Discovering & Defining Insights Guide Step guide · Step 5
6 The Creative Idea — Idea Haus Guide Step guide · optional creative step

UNITED PARTNERS · AI TRANSFORMATION
CD-S-002
Corporate Reputation Strategy, Built From Scratch
The 11-Step AI-Aligned Process · the master specification the AI transformation team follows
Integrated master — the CD-S-002 from-scratch workflow enriched with the AI-Aligned Process spec  
(deliverables, formats, gates, AI/human split).
Measurement standard: AMEC Barcelona Principles 4.0 + AMEC IEF
About this document
This is the master specification for building a corporate communications strategy the United Partners way — 
and the blueprint the AI automation must follow step for step. It integrates two source documents into one: the 
CD-S-002 from-scratch workflow (the reasoning spine and the Enterprise/SME and B2B/B2C forks) and the AI-
Aligned Process (the per-step purpose, frameworks, AI/human split, quality gate, deliverable and document 
format).
From-scratch premise. Nothing about positioning, narrative or pillars is pre-decided — the workflow reasons to 
them from evidence. The spine is identical for all clients; the branch blocks show where the path forks for 
Enterprise vs. SME and B2B vs. B2C.
Two principles the engine must never break
1 · AI raises the floor, the human sets the ceiling. Every step has an explicit AI-drafts / human-owns split. The 
engine generates volume, checks line-of-sight and enforces the gates; a person judges, interprets, chooses the 
ownable idea and signs. No insight, approach, narrative, platform or impact claim ships on autopilot.
2 · Nothing advances that cannot trace up the chain. Business objective → communication objective → 
strategic approach → narrative → messages → pillars → platform → tactics → KPIs. Every quality gate tests this 
line of sight; anything orphaned goes to the appendix, never the strategy.
Legend
Marker Meaning
Core spine Applies to all clients
Enterprise / SME Fork by client size
B2B / B2C Fork by market
GATE Review gate — must pass to advance
DECISION Client-owned call
HARD STOP No downstream work begins until passed
LOCK Scaffold converted into approved strategy
The flow at a glance
Eleven steps, grouped into four movements — Frame, Discover, Build, Activate & Evaluate. The reasoning 
stages of the original CD-S-002 (positioning options, recommend direction, founder elicitation, lock the 
platform, proof discipline) are folded into the matching steps.
Movement Steps
FRAME 1 · Brief from the client   2 · Debrief (Q&A) + founder/executive elicitation   3 · Final brief (locked — the task 
for AI)
DISCOVER 4 · Research & analysis   5 · Frame the problem → Insights defined   (optional) Creative Big Idea — Idea Haus
BUILD 6 · Strategic approach (positioning options → recommend → prioritise)   7 · Narrative, key messages & pillars 
→ LOCK the platform   8 · Communications platform architecture
ACTIVATE & EVALUATE 9 · Engagement plan & execution rollout   10 · Measurement & evaluation   11 · Annual review & update
Cross-cutting.  The Language & Style Standard and the Risks, Guardrails & Proof Discipline (below) apply to 
every step and are enforced at every gate.
Language & Style Standard
Applies to every document at every step. Two decisions govern how the work reads: which language it is 
delivered in, and which voice it is written in. Both are set early, locked in the final brief, and enforced at every 
drafting gate — so a corporate reputation strategy reads as one considered, consistent voice from the brief to 
the scorecard.
Decision 1 — Delivery language
Rule
Default Deliver client-facing documents in the language of the client's primary stakeholders and approval chain. Internal 
engine artifacts (research pack, insight cards, gap registers) are produced in the engine's working language, unless 
the client team works in a local language.
Multi-market Build one core set in the lead language, then localise per market — mirroring the global-toolkit → localised 
principle in Step 9. A small set of global terms stays fixed; local markets adapt language, hooks and proof.
Where it is locked The delivery language(s) is a locked field in the Step 3 final brief. No drafting begins until it is set.
Decision 2 — Voice & style: mirror the client where strong, default to house 
style where not
The strategy should feel native to the client. Where the client already communicates well, we mirror their voice; 
where they don't, we hold the line with the UP house style — and note that a weak or inflated corporate voice 
is often part of the reputation problem the strategy must solve.
Style calibration (Step 1, refined 
in Step 4)
Action
If strong enough Capture a one-page Client Style Note (tone, typical sentence length, vocabulary, how they refer to 
themselves, signature do/don't words) and mirror it across all client-facing deliverables so the strategy 
reads as their own voice.
If not strong enough Default to the UP house style below, and flag the gap — an unclear, jargon-heavy or inflated corporate 
voice is frequently a symptom of the reputation problem, not a neutral choice.
The UP house style (the floor every document meets)
Principle Rule
Plain language Write for a smart reader in a hurry. No jargon; no acronym without its first-use definition; no filler.
Short & active One idea per sentence; active voice; short paragraphs. Speak in headlines, then support them.
Evidence over adjectives Claims carry proof, not superlatives — the proof-first guardrail applies to language, not just content.
Confident, not boastful Warm, not casual; assured, not inflated. No hedging that hides a decision; no claim that outruns its evidence.
Consistent terminology The same thing is called the same name throughout — preserve definitions across every document (the AMEC 
discipline).
Reader-first structure Headline first, then the support beneath it — the Trident 1°→2°→3° logic applied to how every page is written.
How the standard applies by document type
Document type Standard
Internal analytical Research pack, insight cards, gap registers — precise, sourced, plain. Working language. Clarity over polish, 
but never jargon.
Client-facing strategic Brief, one-pager, narrative, message architecture, platform — the client's voice where strong, else UP house 
style. Polished and board-ready.
Execution collateral Releases, social, Q&A, spokesperson materials — the audience's language and the brand narrative voice. On-
template, on-brand, do-not-say lines enforced.
Measurement Scorecard and reports — plain and decision-led. Baseline/target/result/trend always shown; no jargon, no 
inflated attribution.
Enforcement.  The delivery language and the chosen voice (mirror vs house style) are locked in the Step 3 final 
brief; the Client Style Note travels with the engagement and every drafting step references it; the pre-publish 
quality gate in Step 9 and each step's own gate check for language and style compliance before anything 
advances.
Risks, Guardrails & Proof Discipline
A cross-cutting discipline that gives the workflow teeth. It applies from the first build and is checked at every 
gate.
1. Name the primary reputation risks (overclaim, inconsistency, ambiguity).
2. Set the proof-quality ladder: named ref > anon-verifiable > artifact > demo. Place validated proof on the 
ladder; drop what cannot be placed.
3. Assign accountable review gates with named owners GATE.
4. Write the “do-not-say” list — no invented clients, metrics or claims.
5. Set claim-tiering language rules (the attribution wording must match the evidence).
Enforced by the engine.  This discipline is operationalised by the Adversarial Review Board's Competitor, CFO, 
Journalist and GC personas and by the do-not-say lines carried in Steps 7–9 — so weak or unsubstantiated 
claims are caught before they reach a stakeholder.
The Process — eleven steps
Each step sets out its purpose, the frameworks the engine runs, the AI/human split, the quality gate, and the 
exact deliverable and document format. Where the original CD-S-002 adds reasoning detail or a client fork, it is 
folded into the matching step as Process steps and Forks.
FRAME   empty slate → a locked, approved brief
Step 1 —  Brief from the Client
Source guide: Client Intake & Briefing Toolkit (Pass 1 — Prepare). The engine's Frame phase begins here.
Purpose Receive and frame the client's request — but never take the brief at face value. A corporate reputation 
strategy is only as good as the brief beneath it; weak inputs produce a confident, well-structured, wrong 
strategy.
Frameworks & tools The desk-audit pass before any conversation: Business audit, Reputation audit, Social & digital audit, 
Competitive audit, Stakeholder scan, Context scan (regulatory/ESG/geopolitical). Arrive with a hypothesis — a 
provisional point of view on the reputation problem and the white space. Run the Style calibration (read the 
client's own published communications).
What the AI drafts Runs the six pre-conversation audits from public sources; assembles a briefing pack on the company, its 
reputation, its peers and the category; drafts a provisional problem hypothesis and a draft Client Style Note for 
the operator to challenge.
What the human owns Adds the point of view; decides which hypothesis to test; tailors the question bank so every question shows the 
client we already understand them.
Quality gate The desk audit is complete and a written hypothesis exists before any client conversation. “Tailor, don't recite” 
— the question bank is a starting point, not a script.
Deliverable Pre-Engagement Briefing Pack + Provisional Hypothesis (+ draft Client Style Note)
Document format Word document (6 short audit sections + one-paragraph hypothesis), 3–5 pages. Stored in the client folder on 
Google Drive.
Process steps (from CD-S-002 · Phase 1)
1. Capture client type: industry, market, B2B/B2C, size (Enterprise vs SME).
2. State the trigger event and the real business/reputation problem.
3. Set objectives as business outcomes (not positioning).
4. List candidate audiences — unranked at this stage.
5. Define must-say / must-avoid guardrails.
6. Log constraints: legal, regulatory, confidentiality, AI-use limits, anonymization.
7. Name expected outputs and “what good looks like”.
Fork — Brief emphasis forks by client size
Enterprise SME
Parent-group / board constraints captured Founder ambition & constraints captured
Regulatory & disclosure exposure logged Lean, execution-by-small-team framing
Multi-stakeholder approval chain mapped Name/search & discoverability noted early
Step 2 —  Debrief (Q&A) + Founder / Executive Elicitation
Source guide: Client Intake & Briefing Toolkit (Pass 2 — Ask). The structured client conversation(s).
Purpose Extract the maximum useful information from the client — and surface the conflicts between stakeholders — 
through structured, well-prepared conversation. The brief is a battlefield: the CEO wants boldness, the CFO 
wants value, the GC wants safety, HR wants internal-first. Elicit substance — never invent it.
Frameworks & tools The eight-set question bank: A essentials/the ask · B business & organizational context · C reputation & 
stakeholder context · D audience & insight · E programme, narrative & channels · F team, culture & ways of 
working · G constraints & guardrails (incl. AI-use / MNPI) · H logistics & decision process. Technique: open, then 
probe with “why?” and “so what?” until the real answer surfaces. Founder/executive elicitation prompts to 
surface the ownable line and the first ladder-ranked proof point.
What the AI drafts Tailors the question bank to this client from the Step 1 pack; tracks answers against the eight sets in real time; 
flags thin or evasive answers for follow-up; drafts the debrief write-up.
What the human owns Runs the conversation; interviews more than one stakeholder; listens for the unsaid (the tension, the 
hesitation, the downplayed misperception); reflects the problem back before leaving.
Quality gate More than one voice interviewed where possible; the stakeholder conflicts are captured as a Client Alignment 
Map (who wants what, who fears what) — this is what stops the strategy being reversed at executive review.
Deliverable Debrief Write-Up + Client Alignment Map
Document format Word document: structured debrief notes organised by the eight question sets, plus a one-page Alignment 
Map table (stakeholder × wants × fears × conflict). Google Drive.
Founder / Executive elicitation (from CD-S-002 · Phase 10)
1. Run the interview prompts to surface the ownable line.
2. Elicit the first ladder-ranked proof point.
3. Ask what the client walks away from (defines the edge).
4. Draw out why the company exists (origin / purpose).
5. Surface where leaders disagree on the future story.
Fork — Who sits in the room
Enterprise SME
CCO + CEO + parent-group / regulatory voices Founders / managing partners
Multiple stakeholders; alignment is the output Founders ARE the brand; their words are the source
Step 3 —  Final Brief (the Task for AI)
Source guide: Client Intake & Briefing Toolkit (Pass 3 — Close). This is a hard stop — the cheapest gate in the engine, 
preventing the most expensive failure.
Purpose Reconcile everything gathered, fill or consciously park every gap, and lock a single approved brief — the 
definitive task the AI engine will build the strategy from. No research starts until the brief and the 
measurement brief are approved in writing.
Frameworks & tools The gap register (required field × have it? × source × owner × by when) covering: business problem/objective; 
priority audiences & current state; reputation problem/desired perception; decision-maker & approval path; 
baseline data & measurement access; constraints, guardrails & AI permissions; budget, timeline & markets. The 
final-brief gate + the mandatory Measurement Brief (baseline, target, source, owner — see Step 10). Evidence-
readiness screen (below).
What the AI drafts Assembles the one-page Client Intake Brief from Steps 1–2; maintains the gap register and flags which required 
fields are still empty; drafts the Measurement Brief skeleton.
What the human owns Confirms the problem is stated at reputation/company level — not as a tactic; confirms there are no material 
unknowns; sets the engagement tier, governance and AI-status; secures written approval from the decision-
maker.
Quality gate (HARD STOP) The problem is at company/reputation level; no undisclosed risk remains; tier, governance and AI-status are 
set; the brief AND the measurement brief are approved in writing by the decision-maker. No downstream work 
begins otherwise.
Deliverable Approved One-Page Client Intake Brief + Approved Measurement Brief
Document format Word/PDF: the one-page brief (Client & context; Organizational objective; Reputation problem/opportunity; 
Priority audiences; Desired change; Stakeholders & alignment; Constraints & guardrails; Assets & access; 
Success & measurement; Scope & logistics) + one-page Measurement Brief. Both PDF-locked with written 
approval recorded. Google Drive.
Evidence readiness & gap check (from CD-S-002 · Phase 2)
1. Inventory known, verifiable facts (high-trust inputs).
2. List missing inputs that block a locked strategy.
3. Flag inconsistencies — do not resolve by assertion.
4. Separate fact vs. agency-proposal vs. situation/trigger.
5. Run compliance / MNPI / confidentiality screen GATE.
6. State strategic judgment: is input strong enough for a first build?
DISCOVER   evidence → the one truth the strategy is built on
Step 4 —  Research & Analysis
Source guide: Research & Audit. The golden rule: start from the brief and work forwards to insight. Volume is not the goal; 
relevance is.
Purpose Find the few truths a strategy can be built on — not describe the world. Research is the bridge between the 
locked brief and the Killer Insight, run as a chain, not a data dump.
Frameworks & tools Buckets & Questions (mutually-exclusive categories from the brief, one sharp question each, every one 
surviving the “so what?” test). Communications-PESTLE (reputation lens). Stakeholder mapping on the 
Power/Interest grid. The five audits: Business, Social Media, Mainstream Media, Competitive, Persona. 
Reputation & trust audit (sentiment, SOV on themes, trust drivers, the say-do gap). Modern scans: search/SEO, 
review-mining, regulatory/ESG, geopolitical, vulnerability, optional primary research (5–8 stakeholder dipstick).
What the AI drafts Desk research; drafts each of the five audits; SOV & sentiment analysis; theme & word-cloud extraction; 
persona drafts; PESTLE/regulatory/ESG scans — every finding sourced and dated.
What the human owns Directs what to investigate; validates every source; interprets what findings mean; spots the non-obvious; 
decides what is material; owns the synthesis toward the Sweet Spot.
Quality gate Every bucket has sourced findings; every finding connects to a “so what” (no orphan data); no invented figures, 
every source cited and dated, confidence flagged; PESTLE, stakeholder map and the five audits complete for 
the tier; a candidate Sweet Spot / White Space articulated; the pack reaches at least the Information level of 
the pyramid.
Deliverable The Research & Insight Pack
Document format One structured Word/PDF pack (not five disconnected audits): executive summary (3–5 findings, each with its 
“so what”); bucket-by-bucket sourced findings; Comms-PESTLE + stakeholder map; the five audits; reputation 
& trust read; emerging Sweet Spot/White Space; confidence & limitations. Google Drive.
Step 5 —  Frame the Problem → Insights Defined
Source guide: Discovering & Defining Insights. The most important distinction in the whole engine — a strategy built on a 
fact is a strategy built on sand.
Purpose Turn research into the one previously-unspoken truth about people that, once said, feels obviously true — and 
reveals an opportunity. Data tells you WHAT; an insight tells you WHY it matters and WHAT it means, and 
always carries a tension the strategy can resolve.
Frameworks & tools Insight-or-not calibration; empirical + intuitive insight (prove and discover); the 5 T's (True, Tacit, Touches the 
heart, Tension, Triggers action); the So-What ladder (Data → Information → Insight → Foresight) and the five 
traps; the seven-step extraction process; the Sweet Spot; the Distinctiveness Gate; the Validation Gate (test 
contrarian insights with the real audience). Reputation lens: trust drivers, the say-do gap, the misperception, 
the stakeholder tension.
What the AI drafts Generates many candidate insights (empirical & intuitive) from the research; surfaces supporting evidence; 
runs the So-What ladder, the 5 T's, the traps and the Distinctiveness check; drafts the Killer Insight card.
What the human owns Selects the insight; judges the non-obvious; defines and sharpens the wording; defends it; decides which vetted 
candidate is the one. AI never authors the insight on autopilot.
Quality gate It is an insight, not a fact/statistic/observation; passes all 5 T's; survived the So-What ladder and avoids the five 
traps; sits in the Sweet Spot and passes the Distinctiveness Gate; validated with the audience where 
contrarian; human-owned, sourced, sharply written; no more than three — ideally one.
Deliverable 1–3 Killer Insight Cards (ideally one)
Document format Word/PDF card per insight: the insight (1–2 sentences); type (empirical/intuitive/both); the evidence; the 
tension; the 5 T's check; the audience it's about; the opportunity it opens. Google Drive.
Frame the strategic problem (from CD-S-002 · Phase 3)
1. Distil the core reputation tension (not “low awareness”).
2. Articulate the differentiation problem vs. category.
3. Name the trust / affinity / discoverability gap.
Fork — Problem lens shifts by market
B2B B2C
Buyer trust under high-consideration scrutiny Mass perception, affinity & brand love
Proof, references & founder/exec credibility central Emotional resonance & consistency at scale central
Surface open positioning decisions (from CD-S-002 · Phase 4)
1. List client-owned decisions still open DECISION.
2. List UP-owned strategic judgments to resolve before recommending.
3. Set the proof threshold required before claims go external.
Optional —  The Creative Big Idea (Idea Haus)
Source guide: The Creative Idea — Idea Haus. Optional and dual-use: the overall creative concept, or a self-contained 
campaign-ideation method. It sits between the insight and the strategic approach.
Purpose Turn the insight and strategy into a Big Idea — an elevated purpose, not a tactic. A repeatable process that 
makes the creative floor high and consistent; the strategist still makes the ceiling.
Frameworks & tools The six steps: Internalize the strategy → Result-back thinking → Embrace insights → Elevate the objectives 
(NEED + VALUE = POWER) → Focused ideation (large group → small group → one) → Validate against the Big 
Idea Criteria (Simple, Shareable, Scalable, Memorable, Ownable, Persuasive). Lateral-thinking brain-trainers: 
Random Entry, Provocation, Challenge Idea, Movement.
What the AI drafts Drafts the internalised brief; generates result-back visions; runs the four brain-trainers at volume to produce 
many bold candidate ideas; elevates the objectives; drafts concepts in words + images; validates each against 
the Big Idea Criteria.
What the human owns The creative spark and taste; selects the idea with heart; judges what is ownable and category-breaking; builds, 
elevates and sells it.
Quality gate It is a Big Idea (elevated purpose), not a tactic; flows from the insight, the result-back vision and the elevated 
objective; passes the Big Idea Criteria; is ownable; was generated from many options and pushed with a brain-
trainer; expressed in words + images, ready to build.
Deliverable A Validated Big Idea Concept
Document format Word/PDF concept (words + images): the one-sentence strategic summary, the elevated objective, the Big 
Idea, and the criteria check. Google Drive.
BUILD   the insight becomes an owned, locked strategy
Step 6 —  Strategic Approach
Source guide: Building the Strategic Approach. Where the insight becomes a decision about how to win — the single 
organizing idea for how communications will change what stakeholders think, feel or do.
Purpose Decide the one organizing idea that resolves the insight's tension and moves the objective. Get it right and 
narrative, messages, channels and tactics flow naturally; get it wrong and no execution saves it.
Frameworks & tools The Strategy Blueprint cascade (business objective → communication objective → strategic approach → 
messages/channels/tactics → KPIs, all in line of sight). The SMART+I communication objective. The GET / 
WHO / TO / BY strategic-direction statement + one-line positioning. Reputation = experience − expectations → 
the three moves: Reposition · Close the trust gap · Own the tension. Generate several options; select on Fit, 
Distinctiveness, Feasibility, Line of sight. Reputation building blocks: Identity→Image→Reputation; issue 
management; the stakeholder imperative.
What the AI drafts Drafts SMART+I objectives from the brief; generates several distinct strategic approaches from the insight, 
each with rationale; checks line-of-sight up and down the cascade; drafts the message architecture and the 
one-pager; runs the Distinctiveness check.
What the human owns Chooses the approach; judges the ownable idea; sets the positioning and the stand; confirms fit to the 
company's character and risk appetite; defends it.
Quality gate The communication objective is SMART+I and traces to a business objective; the approach flows directly from 
the insight; expressed as GET/WHO/TO/BY plus one-line positioning; chosen from options and passes the 
Distinctiveness Gate; is one of reposition / close-the-gap / own-the-tension; has clean line of sight up and 
down; captured on the Strategy One-Pager for the tier.
Deliverable The Strategy One-Pager (the north star)
Document format Word/PDF one-pager: executive summary; business & communication objectives (SMART+I); target audience & 
persona; the strategic approach + one-line positioning; core narrative & 3–5 key messages; proof points; 
channel strategy (PESO); campaign timeline & phases; success metrics & KPIs; budget & risk. Google Drive.
Develop positioning options (from CD-S-002 · Phase 5)
1. Build option on the “how the firm works” axis (capability/craft).
2. Build option on the “who vouches” axis (trust/founder/relationship).
3. Build option on the “who the firm is for” axis (vertical/domain).
4. For each: best-fit condition, strength, risk, evidence needed.
Fork — Vertical option plays a different role by size
Enterprise SME
Vertical usually a PROOF LANE beneath a broad master idea Vertical often the LEAD — small proof base dominates a niche faster
Can't lead with a niche it isn't yet recognised for Narrowing is the efficient answer to thin proof
Recommend direction & rationale (from CD-S-002 · Phase 6)
1. Recommend a lead territory (+ supporting layers).
2. Tie recommendation to strongest available evidence.
3. State it as a direction to TEST, not a locked position.
4. Define the condition that would promote/change the lead.
Stakeholder prioritisation (from CD-S-002 · Phase 8)
1. Rank audiences for the first 6–12 months DECISION.
2. Justify each priority against risk & value.
3. Set which audience hears the story first.
Fork — Typical first-priority audience differs
Enterprise SME
Regulators / parent-group / board often first Buyers & referral sources often first
License-to-operate & approval-critical stakeholders Fastest path to commercial reputation value
Step 7 —  Narrative, Key Messages & Content Pillars → LOCK the Platform
Source guide: Narrative, Key Messages & Communications Pillars. One connected message architecture — not three 
separate tasks — flowing from the strategic approach.
Purpose Build the one story with real tension, the messages that carry it to each audience, and the few enduring pillars 
everything ladders to. If a message or pillar doesn't trace back to the narrative, it doesn't belong.
Frameworks & tools NARRATIVE: story planning (context, audience, purpose, how); World → Tension → Resolution; the UP 
Narrative Template (“We believe in a world where… / We know… / So we make sure… / Which is why we…”); 
trailer + tweet compression. KEY MESSAGES: 3–5 distinct, audience-specific; the 6-type Messaging Architecture 
(Awareness, Relevance, Emotion, Logic, Action, Commitment under one umbrella); the Trident ladder (1° → 2° 
→ 3°/killer facts); Message Storming, Testing, Training; do-not-say guardrails. PILLARS: 3–5 ownable territories; 
Hero/Hub/Hygiene balance; story types (Evergreen/Seasonal/Real-time).
What the AI drafts Drafts narrative options from the insight & approach using the template; generates key messages by audience 
with proof; proposes pillars mapped to the narrative; ladders messages; drafts the trailer and tweet; checks 
every message and pillar traces to the narrative.
What the human owns Owns the story truth and its tension; judges what's ownable vs generic; chooses the narrative; approves 
messages and proof; sets the do-not-say lines; decides the pillars.
Quality gate The narrative has genuine tension and uses the template; is ownable and compresses to a trailer and a tweet; 
key messages are 3–5, distinct, audience-specific, each with proof; messages are laddered and carry do-not-say 
guardrails; 3–5 pillars each tracing to the narrative and a message; pillars balanced Hero/Hub/Hygiene and 
classified by story type; everything ladders to the one narrative — no orphans.
Deliverable The Message Architecture (Narrative + Key Messages + Pillars)
Document format Word/PDF: the narrative (template + trailer + tweet); the Key-Message set by audience with laddered proof 
and do-not-say lines; the 3–5 pillars mapped to narrative, message and story type. Google Drive.
Message architecture — first build (from CD-S-002 · Phase 7)
1. Draft the working core idea (kept as “to lock”).
2. Build narrative pillars — each with role, audiences, proof-to-validate, do-not-say.
3. Map audience-specific proof tracks.
4. List the decisions required to lock it.
Fork — Channel & pillar weighting forks by market
B2B B2C
Owned proof + founder/exec visibility + LinkedIn/thought leadership 
lead
Earned + shared/social + community/CSR lead
Referral & partner-ecosystem tracks weighted Consumer affinity & brand-consistency tracks weighted
1. Insert the client's own ownable phrase (their words, not tidied).
2. Place validated proof on the ladder; drop what can't be placed.
3. Approve core idea, pillars, proof, stakeholder priority DECISION.
4. Pass final approval / sign-off gate GATE.
Step 8 —  Communications Platform Architecture
Source guide: The Communications Platform — Channels & Tactics. The unifying architecture that turns strategy, narrative 
and messages into an organized, integrated system — not a list of activities.
Purpose Build the organizing logic that makes every channel and tactic reinforce one story and one insight. If your 
channels could each belong to a different strategy, you have a list, not a platform.
Frameworks & tools The five platform criteria (differentiation, heritage, extension, competitive advantage, durable/global). The 
pull-through line of sight (Vision/Position → Brand Expression → Go-to-Market → Communications Programs). 
PESO orchestrated around one insight — earned-led for reputation; the 4C integrated programming model; the 
Pyramid of Influence. Every tactic mapped to audience × message × pillar and built as an Activation Card 
(Insight → Idea → Engagement → Outcome + KPI + phase).
What the AI drafts Generates candidate platforms and tests them against the five criteria; maps tactics to 
audiences/messages/pillars; drafts Activation Cards; builds the PESO plan; checks every tactic for line of sight; 
drafts the Communications Plan.
What the human owns Chooses the platform; judges what's ownable and integrated; sets channel priorities and the earned-led 
balance; approves the tactics; owns feasibility, budget and risk.
Quality gate The platform passes the five criteria; every channel and tactic traces up to an audience, a message and the 
objective; PESO is integrated around one insight (earned-led), not four silos; every tactic is an Activation Card 
with a KPI and a phase; the architecture is ownable and durable.
Deliverable The Communications Platform (integrated architecture)
Document format Word/PDF: the platform idea + why it's ownable (five-criteria check); the PESO channel architecture (earned-
led); the audience × message × pillar × channel × tactic map; the tactics as Activation Cards. Google Drive.
ACTIVATE & EVALUATE   strategy → ready-to-run activity → proven outcome → refreshed strategy
Step 9 —  Engagement Plan & Execution Rollout
Source guides: The Communications Platform (engagement model) + The Execution Toolkit. Campaigns and always-on — 
executable by any team without the strategist in the room.

5. Language requirements — every document, no exceptions
Every document we deliver must be simple, professional and understandable — in its wording and as a whole 
text. A strategy that cannot be understood at first reading is not finished. These requirements apply to all 
documents, internal and client-facing, and are checked at every gate.
5.1 The wording — sentence by sentence
Requirement Rule
Plain words Use the everyday word, not the impressive one. No jargon. No acronym without its meaning at first use. No filler.
Short sentences One idea per sentence. Active voice. If a sentence needs a second read, rewrite it.
Concrete, not abstract Say what happens, who does it, and by when. Replace vague claims with facts.
Proof, not adjectives Every claim carries evidence. Delete superlatives that carry none.
Confident, not inflated Assured, warm, direct. No hedging that hides a decision; no claim that outruns its proof.
One name per thing Call the same thing by the same name in every document. Never rename a concept midway.
Reader's language, not the 
method's
Client-facing documents are written in the reader's language, not the method's — the frameworks run the kitchen, but 
the menu is in plain words. No process term (lock, disposition, quarantine, proof pair) reaches a client page 
unexplained.
5.2 The whole text — how the document reads end to end
Requirement Rule
One clear purpose The reader knows in the first paragraph what this document is and what it is for.
Headline first Every section starts with its point, then the support beneath it. A busy reader who reads only the headings still gets the 
story.
Logical flow Sections follow one order of thought. Each builds on the one before. No jumps, no repeats.
Right length As short as the content allows. Anything that supports but does not advance the argument goes to an appendix.
Visual clarity Tables for comparisons, short lists for sequences, bold sparingly. White space is part of the writing.
Self-contained A new reader can use the document without a briefing. Terms, context and next steps are inside it.
5.3 The test before any document ships
The plain-language check — run at every gate
  ☐ Could a smart reader outside our industry understand every sentence at first reading?
  ☐ Does every section start with its point? Do the headings alone tell the story?
  ☐ Is there any jargon, unexplained acronym, filler or empty superlative left? Remove it.
  ☐ Does every claim carry its proof?
  ☐ Is the document as short as it can be while still complete?
  ☐ Is every client-facing page in the reader's language — no unexplained process terms?
  ☐ Would you be comfortable reading it aloud to the client's board?

Client Intake & Briefing Toolkit
How to collect the maximum information from the client before finalising the brief
The engine's Frame phase (Steps 1–3) in practice — because a corporate reputation strategy is only as  
good as the brief beneath it.
July 2026 · adapts the MSLGROUP Prospect Call Toolkit for corporate reputation
Why this matters
The brief is the foundation the whole strategy stands on. Every stress test of the engine found the same thing: 
weak inputs produce a confident, well-structured, wrong strategy. Collecting the maximum useful information — 
and reconciling it — before the brief is finalised is the single highest-leverage thing an operator does. This toolkit 
makes that repeatable, so a junior gathers the same depth a senior would.
The one principle (from the MSL Prospect Call Toolkit)
A question bank is a starting point, not a script. Research the brand, industry and market before you ask, so 
every question demonstrates that you already understand them — and provokes a sharper answer. Tailor, 
don't recite.
Where the AI engine helps.  The engine runs the pre-conversation research for you (§2), so you arrive informed 
and ask fewer, better questions. It also tracks which brief fields are still empty (§6), so nothing material is missed 
regardless of who's running the intake.
The three passes
PASS 1 · PREPARE   do your homework before you ask — arrive with a point of view (Step 1).
PASS 2 · ASK   the structured client conversation(s) — the question bank (Step 2).
PASS 3 · CLOSE   debrief, fill the gaps, reconcile, validate and approve the final brief (Step 3).
Pass 1 — Prepare: arrive informed
Before any client conversation, complete a rapid desk audit so your questions show knowledge and target the 
gaps. The engine drafts each of these; you validate and add the point of view.
Audit What to establish before the call
Business audit What the company does, its model, performance, leadership, ownership, recent news, annual report / investor 
materials
Reputation audit Current media coverage — volume, sentiment, narratives, share of voice; rankings; any past crises or live issues
Social & digital audit Channels, presence, tone of voice, community, executive visibility
Competitive audit How 3–5 peers position and communicate; their narrative, thought-leadership and share of voice; the white space
Stakeholder scan Who matters (investors, regulators, employees, media, communities, NGOs); who's talking; advocates and critics
Context scan Regulatory, ESG/CSRD, geopolitical and category forces shaping the operating environment
Come with a hypothesis.  Arrive with a provisional point of view on the reputation problem and the white space. 
A hypothesis you invite the client to correct extracts far more than an open “tell us about your business.”
Pass 2 — Ask: the question bank
Eight sets, adapted from the MSL toolkit for corporate reputation. Use what fits; go deep where the answers are 
thin. Ask open, then probe with “why?” and “so what?” until you reach the real answer.
A. The essentials — the ask
● What exactly is the ask, in one sentence?
● What is the budget — and does that include out-of-pocket / third-party costs?
● Is this a competitive process? How many firms, and roughly what size?
● Why did you include United Partners? What specifically attracted you to us?
● What criteria will you use to evaluate the proposals?
● Who are the key decision-makers, and who gives final approval?
● How will you define success — and by when?
B. Business & organizational context  (feeds the organizational objective)
● Walk us through your business model and how you make money.
● What are your business goals, objectives and priorities — and are they changing in the coming year?
● What single thing most needs to change for the organization, and by when?
● What will stop you achieving these objectives? What are your key business challenges?
● What are your top three KPIs?
● Where do you want to take this company over the next 3–5 years?
● What do you see as your biggest opportunities this year and beyond?
● How does communications and PR fit your wider marketing and business mix?
C. Reputation & stakeholder context  (the heart of a reputation brief)
● How is the company regarded today — by each key stakeholder group?
● What do you most want to be known for? What's the gap between that and today's perception?
● What is the single biggest misperception about your firm?
● Where is the gap between what you say and what you demonstrably do? (the greenwashing/credibility risk)
● Who are your greatest advocates? Who are your critics?
● What reputational risks or vulnerabilities keep you up at night?
● What's your current standing on trust, and how do you know?
● Any regulatory, ESG or sustainability commitments the reputation must stand behind?
● Have you faced any issues or crises? How were they handled and what remains?
D. Audience & insight
● Who are the priority audiences, internally and externally? How do you prioritise them?
● What is each audience's current state — what do they know, feel and do today?
● What must they know, feel or do differently for this to succeed?
● What do they truly care about, and what drives their decisions?
● Do you have audience research, tracking or data we can use? Can we access it?
E. Programme, narrative & channels
● Do you have a clear corporate narrative or story — or will we build one together?
● Who are your spokespeople? How visible are your leaders willing to be?
● How do you rate your strength at media relations, social, strategy and thought leadership?
● Which programmes or initiatives have worked well? What hasn't?
● Sector-specific programmes, one overarching platform, or a bit of both?
● What's your ideal earned-media placement, and what's the headline?
● Anything you don't want to be pitched or associated with?
● What's missing today, from your perspective?
F. Team, culture & ways of working  (surfaces internal politics)
● Tell us about your role and focus, and about your internal team — roles and strengths.
● Who on your side will interface with us most? Who must be kept close beyond them?
● What prompted this search? Do you have an agency today, and why change?
● What does the perfect agency relationship look like to you?
● Where do the CEO, CFO, General Counsel and HR see this differently? Any works-council or internal-approval 
steps we should know?
● What would make this a success for you personally?
Interview more than one person.  The brief is a battlefield: the CEO wants boldness, the CFO wants value, the GC 
wants safety, HR wants internal-first. Speak to several stakeholders where you can — the conflicts you surface 
here become the Client Alignment Map that stops the strategy being reversed at executive review.
G. Constraints & guardrails
● Any commercial, regulatory, legal or reputational constraints on what we can say or do?
● Anything that is off-limits — words, claims, topics, comparisons?
● AI-use permissions: what can and cannot be processed in AI tools? Any material non-public information?
● Is the company listed, in a quiet period, or subject to disclosure rules?
● Is there anything you're not telling us that we'd regret not knowing?
H. Logistics & decision process
● Preferred deliverable format?
● Who will be in the room, in what role, and will the final decision-maker attend?
● Timeline, key dates and relevant markets?
● What access can you give us — analytics, CRM, sales, survey data — for measurement baselines?
Techniques to get more, and better
● Research first. Every question should show you already know the brand, industry and market.
● Open, then probe. Ask broad, then ladder down with “why?” and “so what?” until you reach the real 
answer, not the rehearsed one.
● Talk to several people. One contact gives one truth; the C-suite gives the real, conflicting picture.
● Ask for documents and data. Annual report, research, tracking, past campaigns, and analytics/CRM 
access — evidence beats opinion.
● Listen for the unsaid. The tension, the hesitation, the misperception they downplay — that's often 
where the insight lives.
● Reflect back. Play the problem back in your words before you leave — misunderstandings surface 
immediately.

1. Purpose & the golden rule
Research is the engine's Navigation and Discovery input (CUBE Faces 1–2, flow Step 4). Its job is not to describe 
the world — it is to find the few truths a strategy can be built on. Volume is not the goal; relevance is.
The golden rule
Start from the brief and work forwards to insight. Every piece of research must earn its place by 
answering a question the strategy needs. If a finding can't be connected to the brief or to a “so what,” it 
belongs in the appendix — not the research pack.
Two non-negotiables (from Turning Data Into Insights).  Start with ready data from real sources, and never 
make up data. Every finding carries a source. This is what lets a junior produce research a senior would trust — 
and what the Adversarial Review Board's Journalist persona enforces.
2. Where it sits — from brief to insight
Research is the bridge between the locked brief and the Killer Insight. It runs as a chain, not a data dump:

4. The discipline that makes research strategic — Buckets & 
Questions
Buckets stop research becoming an unfocused data hunt. They are categories drawn from the brief; each gets 
one strategic question; each question must survive the “so what?” test.
Worked micro-example
Bucket: Reputation & trust drivers.
Question: Which trust dimension is the company weakest on with its priority audience, and why?
So-what test: “If I know the weakest trust driver, I can aim the whole strategy at closing it.” → strategic. 
Keep it.
Principles: buckets are mutually exclusive; clearly defined (not too broad, not too narrow); refined as you learn; 
and can be broad (Reputation, Audience) or narrow (Trust among regulators). Add new buckets when the data 
reveals a theme you didn't expect.

Discovering & Defining Insights
The AI-Transformation guide to the Insight phase
Phase 3 of the flow (CUBE · Discovery, Step 5). Where research becomes the one truth a strategy is  
built on.
July 2026 · builds on Discovering Insights (5 T's), Turning Data Into Insights, and the WARC buyer-persona method
1. What an insight is — and what it is not
This is the most important distinction in the whole engine. Most “insights” in strategy decks are not insights at all 
— they are facts, statistics or observations. A strategy built on a fact is a strategy built on sand.
Definition
An insight is a previously-unspoken truth about people that, once said, feels obviously true — and 
reveals an opportunity. Data tells you WHAT is happening; an insight tells you WHY it matters and WHAT 
it means. It always carries a tension the strategy can resolve.
Insight… or not?  (calibration)
Train your eye. If it's a number, a company fact, or an activity, it's data — not an insight. If it reveals a human 
truth with tension, it's an insight.
Statement Insight? Why
“80% of users believe Ariel cleans better than any other product.” NO A research statistic — data, not meaning
“The brand is manufactured in the United States.” NO A company fact
“Once they try it, 75% are repeat purchasers.” NO A behavioural data point
“The product is 85% recycled material.” NO A fact about the product
“Women want to look and feel years younger.” WEAK True, but generic and unspoken by no one — no 
tension, not ownable
“Women love the moment at night when the dishes are finally clean.” YES An unspoken human truth with emotion and 
tension — an insight
2. Two kinds of insight — and why you need both
Empirical insight Intuitive insight
What it is Grounded in data acquired through research methods Grounded in knowing or sensing, without a rational process
Example “Heavy users are 3× more likely to own a dog.” “She still wants a fairy-tale ending.”
Proven by The data itself Observation and qualitative evidence — it still needs backup
The UP principle.  “It is through science that we prove, but through intuition that we discover.” The strongest 
Killer Insights pair an intuitive human truth with empirical proof — the discovery and the evidence together.
3. The quality bar — the 5 T's
A candidate is only a Killer Insight if it passes all five. This is the test a novice and a veteran apply identically — 
which is what makes insight quality operator-independent.
The 5 T's
True — grounded in reality and evidence; not a guess.
Tacit — unspoken; people feel it but rarely say it out loud.
Touches the heart — it has emotional resonance, not just logic.
Tension — it holds a conflict or gap that demands resolution.
Triggers action — it points clearly to what the strategy should do.
4. The climb — from data to insight
Insight is a level on a ladder, reached by disciplined questioning — not a lucky thought.
Level What it is
Data Raw, uncontextualised facts (“sales rose 23%”)
Information Data organised & compared (“23% — 5 points above target, 8 below history”)
Insight What it means, strategically (“the growth is masking a loyalty problem”)
Foresight What it signals for the future (“expect margin pressure in 12 months”)
The tool that climbs it: the So What? test. For every finding ask “so what?” and keep asking until you reach 
genuine meaning. Guard against the five traps: correlation mistaken for causation · confirmation bias · volume 
mistaken for significance · the missing counterfactual · outliers mistaken for trends.
5. The extraction process — seven steps
Step What you do Tool
1  Immerse Absorb the Research & Insight pack — the filled buckets, the audits, the reputation 
read
Research pack
2  Generate volume Write MANY candidate insights about the WHO — empirical and intuitive. Dig past 
the obvious; don't edit yet
Empirical / Intuitive worksheet
3  So-What ladder Push each promising candidate up the pyramid with repeated “so what?” Insight Pyramid + So What
4  Screen Test each against the 5 T's; discard anything that isn't True, Tacit, heart-touching, 
tension-holding and action-triggering
The 5 T's
5  Find the Sweet Spot Cross candidates with the Sweet Spot: the company's ownable truth ∩ an insight not 
yet leveraged ∩ what the audience truly cares about
Sweet Spot
6  Distinctiveness Gate Reject any insight a competitor could also claim, or that's the obvious white space 
everyone sees
Distinctiveness Gate

Volume first, then judgment.  Great insight comes from generating many candidates and then ruthlessly filtering 
— not from waiting for one perfect thought. The AI is excellent at the volume; the human owns the filtering and 
the final call.
6. Defining it — how to write a Killer Insight
An insight badly written is an insight wasted. Keep it human, sharp, one or two sentences, and make the tension 
visible. Useful forms:
Insight forms
Human-truth form: “[Audience] believe/feel [X], but the truth is [Y] — which the company can resolve by 
[Z].”
Tension form: “In a world where [context], [audience] want [A] yet fear [B].”
Reputation form (corporate): “What tension must this company resolve in the eyes of its stakeholders to 
earn trust, grow, or protect its licence to operate?”
Worked example (AUBG, reputation)
Killer Insight card
Insight: In a region that tells its brightest young people they must leave to succeed, they are proof they 
don't have to — a globally-recognised education that makes you a leader where it matters most: here.
Type: Intuitive truth + empirical proof (brain-drain data, alumni outcomes).
5 T's: True (data) · Tacit (families feel it, rarely say it) · Touches the heart (belonging) · Tension (leave vs 
stay) · Triggers action (position as “rise here”).
Opportunity: Own the reputation of the institution that keeps and grows the region's talent.
7. Audience & persona insight — go beyond demographics
Profiles are not personas. A profile is demographics, role and pain points — a starting point. A persona is defined 
by behaviour: when, how and why people decide. Insight lives in the behaviour, not the demographics.
Buyer / stakeholder PROFILE Buyer / stakeholder PERSONA
Demographics, role, seniority, firmographics, stated pain points Decision triggers, success factors, evaluation process, decision criteria, 
perceived barriers, trusted sources
Map the decision journey — six questions
● Who is involved in the decision?
● Why are they considering it — the triggers and success factors?
● What are they trying to learn — decision criteria and perceived barriers?
● When do they look at different kinds of information?
● How will they evaluate the options?
● Where do they find and trust information?
Two rules from the field.  Think outside-in (the audience's language and concerns), not inside-out (the 
company's features). And “share the insights, not the personas” — a persona is a carrier for 20–30 usable 
insights; it's the insights that drive the work.
8. The reputation lens
For a corporate reputation strategy the “buyer” is every material stakeholder, and the insight is the tension the 
company must resolve to earn standing and trust. Beyond consumer truths, look specifically at:
● Trust drivers — where the company is weak on competence, integrity, purpose or reliability, and why
● The say-do gap — where the narrative outruns demonstrable behaviour (the credibility/greenwashing 
tension)
● The misperception — the single biggest gap between how the company is seen and how it wants to be seen
● The stakeholder tension — the conflict the company sits inside that, if resolved, changes its reputation
9. The two gates — before the insight locks
Distinctiveness Gate: is it ownable (no competitor could claim it), non-obvious (not the white space everyone 
sees), and does it carry a tension appropriate to this company's character?
Validation Gate (Step 5B): a distinctive, contrarian insight cannot lock until it is tested against the real audience 
— the more contrarian it is, the more it must be validated. Confirm / Refine / Reject. Distinctiveness and 
wrongness look identical until tested.
Human-owned, always.  AI generates candidates, surfaces the evidence, and runs the So-What, 5 T's, traps and 
distinctiveness checks. The final insight is chosen, defined and defended by a person. The engine hands the 
human vetted options — it never authors the insight on autopilot.
10. What the AI does, and what the human owns
The AI does The human owns
Generates many candidate insights (empirical & intuitive) from the

Why this is operator-independent.  The tests — Insight-or-not, the 5 T's, So-What, Distinctiveness, Validation — 
are checkable procedures, and the operator chooses from vetted, evidenced candidates rather than originating

judgment.
11. Output & quality gate
The phase produces 1–3 Killer Insight cards, each with: the insight (1–2 sentences), its type (empirical / intuitive / 
both), the evidence, the tension, the 5 T's check, the audience it's about, and the opportunity it opens.
Gate — before the insight goes to Idea (Step 6)
  ☐ It is an insight, not a fact, statistic or observation
  ☐ It passes all 5 T's (True, Tacit, Touches the heart, Tension, Triggers action)
  ☐ It survived the So-What ladder and avoids the five traps
  ☐ It sits in the Sweet Spot and passes the Distinctiveness Gate
  ☐ It is validated with the audience where contrarian (Step 5B)
  ☐ It is human-owned, sourced, and written sharply enough to build on
  ☐ There are no more than three — ideally one
Bottom line. An insight is not what you found — it's what it means. Generate many candidates, prove the 
empirical and discover the intuitive, filter hard with the 5 T's and the So-What ladder, find the ownable Sweet 
Spot, validate the bold ones, and land one sharp human truth with tension. Do that, and the insight a junior 
defines is the same one a 30-year strategist would build the whole strategy on — which is exactly the point of 
this phase.

The Idea Haus — AI-Transformation guide (Step 6, optional)
A repeatable process for unleashing boundless creativity — for the overall creative concept, or for

July 2026 · builds on the MSLGROUP Idea Haus and Delivering Creativity method
1. What the Idea Haus is — and when to use it
The Idea Haus is a repeatable creative process that lets any team design and deliver big ideas — consistently, not 
by luck. Clients increasingly ask for big, game-changing ideas, and don't much care which agency brings them; the 
Idea Haus is how UP delivers them every time. Creativity without structure is chaos; the Idea Haus is creativity 
with structure.
Optional — and dual-use.  This step is optional in the flow. Use it for the overall creative concept / platform that 
expresses the strategy, or as a self-contained method for campaign ideation and planning. Either way it turns the 
insight and strategy into a Big Idea.
2. A Big Idea, not a tactic
The most common creative failure is presenting a tactic dressed up as an idea. A Big Idea is the elevated purpose; 
a tactic is the activity that serves it.
Tactic (what you do) Big Idea (why it matters)
Provide feminine-hygiene products Help young girls in Africa stay in school
Add a new ingredient to increase flavour (the elevated purpose the ingredient serves)
Secure top-tier media / a celebrity A movement of thousands who change a behaviour
The Big Idea Criteria — validate every concept against these
Simple · Shareable (any-size screen) · Scalable · Memorable / recognisable asset · Ownable · Persuasive
A true Big Idea is also: about the brand's purpose/benefit · stands out in its category · radically opens hearts and minds 
· creates movement.
3. The Idea Haus — six steps
Step What it does Output
1  Internalize the strategy Live and breathe the brief — WHO, WHAT (from → to), HOW A one-sentence strategic 
summary
2  Result-back thinking Start at the end — visualise the epic outcome Top 3 visions of success
3  Embrace insights Empirical + intuitive truths about the WHO (the 5 T's) 3 killer insights (see the Insight 
guide)
4  Elevate the objectives Push the client's ask to its biggest version Elevated objectives
5  Focused ideation Generate many ideas, select and build 1 Big Idea concept
6  Validate the concept Check against the Big Idea Criteria A validated Big Idea
Step 1 — Internalize the strategy (the brief)
The creative brief structure
Challenge: what consumer/stakeholder behaviour or mindset change do we hope to achieve?
Insight starters: why are they behaving this way? why should they care? why would they change? why is it 
relevant to their life?
Benefit: what core thing do we promise them — and why would they tell a friend?
Then write it down: WHO (and how we relate to / change them) · WHAT (from what mindset → to what) · HOW 
(how we deliver it) → one sentence. Look. Internalize. Write.
Step 2 — Result-back thinking
Start at the end. With eyes closed, picture the campaign as a movie and visualise how it ends — if we could have 
any ending possible, what would it be? Every outlet talking about it? A movement of thousands? A million 
engaged? Rate the possible outcomes and pick the top three.
Securing media is not a big ending.  “Top-rated media placements” or “a celebrity at an event” are not big 
endings — they're tactics. Push for endings that are epic: movements, behaviour change, cultural impact. Score 
outcomes across Media / Movement / Engagement / Content / WOM / Influencers / Social / Events / Purpose / 
Cause and Local→Global.
Step 3 — Embrace insights
Big ideas are driven by real, impactful insights — empirical (proven by data) and intuitive (sensed, then 
evidenced) — each passing the 5 T's: True, Tacit, Touches the heart, Tension, Triggers action. A “day in the life” 
of the audience is a fast way to surface them. (Covered fully in the Insight guide.)
Step 4 — Elevate the client's objectives
Big ideas mean big objectives. Take what the client asked for and elevate it. “If you don't know where you're 
going, any road will get you there.” We can always scale down.
NEED + VALUE = POWER
What is the client asking for, really?   +  What is the value we add?   =  the elevated objective.
e.g. “Drive trial” → “Place the brand at the centre of ongoing conversations that make trial irresistible.”
Step 5 — Focused ideation
Generate, then focus. Run it large group → small group:
● Set the stage — share the strategy, the result-back vision, the insights and the elevated objectives.
● Ideate — break into small teams; generate freely; capture everything on Post-its; go for quantity.
● Share & evaluate — play ideas back; assess against the criteria.
● Select 3 → build — the ideas you have the most heart for; build each (~10 min per idea).
● Small group → 1 — push outside the norm, pick the one with most potential, build it, express it in 
words + images.
Ask throughout: how do we achieve the end result? how do we bring the insights to life? how do the elevated 
objectives take shape? are the Big-Idea elements present?
Step 6 — Validate the concept
Check the Big Idea, literally box by box, against the Big Idea Criteria. Missing any? Go back and rework the idea to 
include it. Only a validated idea proceeds.
4. Fuel the ideation — lateral-thinking brain-trainers
When ideas go stale or obvious, break the pattern (Edward de Bono's lateral thinking). Four trainers to unlock 
bolder ideas:
Brain-trainer How it works
Random Entry Pick a random word/object unrelated to the task; list what's true about it; force-fit those truths onto the challenge
Provocation Distortion (distort the challenge), Illusionary (exaggerate the payoff to an ideal), Reversal (ask the opposite of the 
problem, then turn it back). The burger “take it away” idea won a Cannes Lion
Challenge Idea Appoint someone to keep asking “Why?” — list your assumptions about the client's business and challenge each 
one
Movement Extract the principle from another example (e.g. Apple's launch playbook) and apply it to your challenge — 
corporate ↔ consumer cross-pollination
This is the engine's creativity engine.  These brain-trainers are exactly the systematic creativity (M6) that fixes 
the weak spot the bake-off found. The AI can run Random Entry, Provocation, Challenge and Movement at 
volume — generating many bold options — while the human selects the one with the spark.
5. Run a great session
The ten ground rules
● Show up · Read the brief · No censoring · It's OK to be silly
● Practise active listening · Build on each other's ideas
● Use “How can we?” or “I wish…” language · Speak in headlines
● Be current · Blue-sky thinking
Environment & facilitation
● Time pressure is a myth. Harvard research: people are LEAST creative under deadline pressure, with a 
two-day hangover. Creativity needs an incubation period — time to soak in the problem.
● Set the room and the invite. Make the invite fun; mix different perspectives; give pre-work that gets 
people into the audience's head; dress the room with thought-starters; serve food; go for quantity; 
write everything down.
6. Package & present the idea
A big idea badly presented dies in the room. Six principles for selling it:
● Be visual and aspirational — show the idea, don't just describe it.
● Tell a story — take the client on a journey.
● You are the star — never read off the slide; if the audience can read your script, they no longer need 
you.
● Sell the idea, not the tactics — lead with the Big Idea; tactics come after.
● Help the client see it boundlessly — show how far the idea can stretch.
● Prop it up — props, costumes, a creative leave-behind to make it memorable.
7. What the AI does, and what the human owns
The AI does The human owns
Drafts the internalised brief and strategic summary; generates result-
back visions; runs the four brain-trainers at volume to produce many 
bold candidate ideas; elevates the objectives; drafts concepts in words 
+ images; validates each against the Big Idea Criteria
Owns the creative spark and taste; selects the idea with heart; judges 
what's ownable and category-breaking; builds and elevates it; sells it in 
the room
Honest boundary.  This is where the human matters most. The engine reliably raises the creative floor — it 
generates volume, breaks patterns, and rejects tactics-masquerading-as-ideas — but the top of the creative 
ceiling is still human. The Idea Haus makes the floor high and consistent; the strategist makes the ceiling.
8. Quality gate — before the idea proceeds
  ☐ It is a Big Idea (an elevated purpose), not a tactic
  ☐ It flows from the insight, the result-back vision and the elevated objective
  ☐ It passes the Big Idea Criteria (simple, shareable, scalable, memorable, ownable, persuasive)
  ☐ It is ownable — a competitor couldn't run the same idea
  ☐ It was generated from many options and pushed with a brain-trainer, not the first thought
  ☐ It is expressed in words + images, ready to build and present
Bottom line. Creativity can be repeatable without being formulaic. Internalize the strategy, imagine the epic 
ending, ground it in a real insight, elevate the objective, generate many ideas and break the pattern with lateral 
thinking, then validate the one Big Idea against the criteria — and sell it as an idea, not a task list. Do that, and a 
junior team lands a genuinely big, ownable idea more often, because the process supplies the discipline and the 
spark supplies the rest.

Phase 4 of the flow (CUBE · Strategy, Step 7). Where the insight becomes a decision about how to win.

1. What the strategic approach is — and why it must be strategic
The strategic approach is the bridge between the insight (what's true) and the plan (what we'll do). It is the single 
organizing idea for HOW communications will change what stakeholders think, feel or do. Get it right and every 
downstream choice — narrative, messages, channels, tactics — flows naturally. Get it wrong and no amount of 
clever execution saves it.
Strategy vs tactics
Tactics are WHAT and HOW — posts, releases, events. Short-term, reactive.
Strategy is WHY and what success looks like — the direction that ties communications to the business. 
Long-term, proactive.
Why this is the hard part.  Only ~26% of communicators say their strategy directly ties to business objectives 
(CMO Council). The strategic approach is where an order-taker becomes a strategic advisor: it asks the diagnostic 
questions, challenges the assumption, and builds the business case — rather than jumping to activity.
2. The Strategy Blueprint — everything must connect
The approach lives inside a cascade with line of sight from the business goal to the metrics. Every level must 
connect to the one above it; if a tactic can't be traced up to the objective, it doesn't belong.
BUSINESS OBJECTIVE   e.g. revenue +15% YoY — what the business must achieve
▼
COMMUNICATION OBJECTIVE   e.g. increase consideration +25% — the shift comms must drive (SMART+I)
▼
STRATEGIC APPROACH   e.g. reposition as the category's innovator — the organizing idea (this step)
▼
MESSAGES · CHANNELS · TACTICS   the narrative, key messages, PESO plan and activities that deliver it
▼
KPIs   how each level is measured back up the chain
3. The Communication Objective (SMART+I)
The approach serves a target. Write it as a SMART+I objective — the difference between a measurable shift and 
an activity.
Letter Test
Specific Clearly defined outcome
Measurable Quantifiable result
Achievable Realistic within resources
Relevant Aligned to the business goal
Time-bound Clear deadline
Impact Drives a business outcome
Example of a strong objective
“Increase brand consideration among the target audience (18–35, urban professionals) by 30% by Q3, 
measured through brand-tracking studies, to drive incremental revenue growth of $2M.”
Objective, not activity.  “Get people to know about us” is an activity. “Shift 45% of stakeholders from unaware to 
actively considering us within 12 months” is an objective. The strategic approach only makes sense once the 
objective is this sharp.
4. Defining the strategic approach itself
The approach is the big organizing idea for how communications will hit the objective — and it must flow directly 
from the insight. The insight named the tension; the approach is the decision about how to resolve it. Articulate 
it two ways:
The strategic-direction statement
GET [the audience]
WHO [their current context / mindset — from the insight]
TO [the shift in what they think, feel or do]
BY [the leverage / organizing idea that makes it happen]
Then a one-line positioning: what the company will stand for, and against, in the eyes of its stakeholders. The 
“BY” and the positioning together are the strategic approach.
The reputation lens
Reputation = experience − expectations (Gary Davies). A reputation approach therefore has only three real 
moves: change the experience, reset the expectations, or close the gap between what the company says and 
what it demonstrably does. Frame the approach as one of: 
● Reposition — claim a new, ownable space (the insight's white space)
● Close the trust gap — attack the specific weak trust driver the research found
● Own the tension — take a defensible stand on the stakeholder tension the insight surfaced
5. Don't take the first idea — generate and select options
Weak strategy is the first plausible approach written up confidently. Strong strategy is chosen from options. Use 
the communications strategy model:
STRATEGIC ANALYSIS   organization–environment · market & competitor · stakeholder (done in Research)
▼
STRATEGIC INTENT   identify the bases of choice · GENERATE several strategic options · evaluate & SELECT
▼
STRATEGIC ACTION   define the role of communications · programme the tactics · organizational arrangements
Selecting between options
Criterion The question
Fit Does it resolve the insight's tension and hit the communication objective?
Distinctiveness Is it ownable — could a competitor run the same approach? (the Distinctiveness Gate)
Feasibility Achievable within budget, timeline, and the company's character and risk appetite?
Line of sight Does it trace cleanly up to the business objective and down to executable tactics?
The engine's role.  This is exactly where the options generator (M5) and the Adversarial Review Board earn their 
place: the AI generates several distinct strategic approaches with rationale; the Board's Competitor persona kills 
the copyable ones; the operator chooses the sharpest — never originating from a blank page, never shipping the 
obvious.
6. Reputation building blocks
For a corporate reputation strategy, the approach draws on a few durable frameworks:
● Identity → Image → Reputation. Reputation is built in phases: corporate identity (what you present) 
shapes image (how you're seen now) which, over time, becomes reputation. The approach must be 
consistent across all three.
● Reputation is holistic. Modern reputation management is strategic, integrated, long-term and involves 
all employees — not just media relations. Build the approach inside-out as well as outside-in.
● Issue management is the backbone. Good reputation management runs on issue management: identify 
→ analyse → choose a change strategy → act → evaluate. Bake the live issues into the approach.
● The stakeholder imperative. The company answers to a plurality of stakeholders, not only shareholders. 
Prioritise them on the power/interest grid and let that shape where the approach concentrates.
● Aim at a real target. Reputation has external yardsticks — RepTrak / Reputation Quotient, Most 
Admired, sustainability indices. Point the approach at a defensible movement on one.

  Part A — The Narrative  (Step 8)
A1. What a narrative is
A brand narrative is the core story you are always telling, in everything you do. It is not a tagline or a message — 
it is the north star beneath them. Strong brands can tell their story a thousand ways and stay recognisable; weak 
brands mean many things and hold nothing together.
The digital-age truth.  In the age of social media, anyone can tell your story and reach a global audience — how 
others tell it now matters more than how you tell it yourself. You can't control the story, but you can shape it to 
be told the way you want. That is what the narrative is for.
A2. Plan the story before you write it
Think of a story as a tree: Story Planning is the roots (why it must be told, and where it lands), the Narrative is 
the trunk, and Story Worlds are the leaves (the elements that adapt over time). Before writing, answer four 
planning questions:
Question How to answer it
What is the context? Survey the external landscape first — communications never happen in a vacuum; how people receive you 
depends on their view of you and what competes for attention
Who is the audience? Think like a journalist (who/what/when/where/why); make them real — a name and a face; write for them, 
not for you
What is the purpose? Awareness (who I am) · Relevance (why I'm here) · Vision (I have a dream) · Education (I'll show you how) · 
Principles-in-action · Dealing with the elephant in the room
How do we tell it? Think like a politician — be Specific, Authentic, Engaging, Appropriate; use real language and real examples, not 
jargon or statistics; repeat with discipline
A3. The narrative structure — World, Tension, Resolution
Every narrative has three movements. Something must be at stake, or there is no story. The company's 
commitment grounds the narrative; the tension is built from what it is willing to do to keep that commitment.
The four-part construction
1 · The world — the world where the focus plays out.
2 · What's at stake — the tension in that world.
3 · What we understand — the truth we grasp about it.
4 · Our role to resolve the tension — what the company does about it.
A4. The UP Narrative Template
The fill-in that turns the structure into a draft. Complete it, then hand it to the copywriters to bring to life.
The Narrative Template (the “Brand Contract”)
We believe in a world where… (the Purpose, as a belief about the world)
We know in that world that… (what we know that brings tension — what's at stake)
So we make sure… (what the company does to resolve the tension)
Which is why we… (the products, services and behaviours that keep the contract)
A5. Make it travel — trailer and tweet
In the digital age the same story is told second by second in “beats.” Compress the narrative so it moves:
● The movie-trailer technique: capture the world, the protagonist and the quest — but not the resolution 
— to pull people into the longer story.
● The tweet: force the whole story into one line. If you can't, it isn't sharp enough yet.
Worked example (the classic Fairy narrative).  “In a world that often pulls people apart, there is one place that 
brings families together: the kitchen. Sometimes things go wrong… But it's also where the small things of family 
life happen. And Fairy is always there — it's our job to keep the kitchen going.” Trailer: “One place brings families 
together again and again. The kitchen.”

1. What a communications platform is
A communications platform is the unifying architecture that turns the strategy, narrative and messages into an 
organized, integrated system of channels and tactics. It is not a list of activities — it is the foundation that 
organizes messaging, priorities and programs into rollout strategies, target audiences, channels and a timeline. It 
is both educational and inspirational, and it is driven by differentiation.
The test of a platform vs a plan.  A plan is a list of things to do. A platform is the organizing logic that makes 
those things add up — so every channel and tactic reinforces one story and one insight. If your channels could 
each belong to a different strategy, you have a list, not a platform.
2. What makes a good platform — the criteria
A strong platform passes five tests (and you should generate several candidate platforms, narrow to two or 
three, and validate with stakeholders before finalising):
● Delivers differentiation — it is ownable, not generic.
● Leverages heritage — it is rooted in what's true about the company.
● Creates extension opportunities — it can stretch across markets, moments and years.
● Sustains competitive advantage — it holds up against what competitors do.
● Is evolutionary, durable and global — it lasts and travels; it isn't a one-campaign idea.
3. Line of sight — the pull-through
The platform connects the brand all the way to the programs, so nothing is orphaned. Every channel and tactic 
must trace up this chain to the strategic approach and the narrative.

▼

▼
GO-TO-MARKET   who you focus on — target audiences, geographies, priority segments
▼
COMMUNICATIONS PROGRAMS   how you communicate — the channels, tactics and activations (this phase)
The rule.  If a tactic can't be traced up to an audience, a message, and the objective, it doesn't go in the platform 
— it goes in the appendix.
4. The channel architecture — PESO, orchestrated
Communications don't live in four separate channel reports. The platform orchestrates Paid, Earned, Shared and 
Owned around one insight, each doing the job it does best. For corporate reputation, the platform is usually 
earned-led — third-party credibility is what builds trust.

Earned Third-party credibility & validation — the reputation engine LEAD

Channels (Earned/Shared/Owned) → Engage Influencers → Develop Compelling Content → Evaluate &

Middle (semi-pro creators, sector voices) → Super Fans & Employees → Fans & Followers. For corporate 
reputation the highest-value influencers are usually credible third parties — analysts, editors, respected alumni 
or partners — and employees as advocates.

July 2026 · builds on v1.0
What it is — and its honest boundary
After the engine drafts a strategy (or a key artifact), a panel of AI personas each attacks it from a specific 
adversary's point of view — the people who, in the real world, would try to tear it apart. The strategy must 
survive them. This is how a novice operator gets the same scrutiny a 30-year strategist would apply, 
without a strategist present.
The honest boundary.  The Board delivers senior-grade SCRUTINY — it finds the problems a senior would find. It 
does not deliver senior-grade CREATION — it doesn't originate the brilliant fix. Pair it with the options generator 
(M5/M6): the Board finds the flaw, the generator proposes fixes, the operator chooses. And it tests logic and 
exposure, not ground truth — so real audience validation (M7) stays essential; the Board can't catch a wrong-
but-plausible insight if the data feeding it is wrong.
1. Where it runs
Placement Board convened Why here
Insight mini-board (Step 5B) Competitor + Target Audience + Activist Kill a weak insight before a whole strategy is
